overview.title: Foreign Banks
overview.definition: Foreign banks are banking institutions headquartered in a foreign country that operate branches, subsidiaries, or representative offices within India under the regulatory framework of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) and the Banking Regulation Act, 1949.
overview.importanceInUpsc: Frequently tested in Prelims regarding RBI regulations, WTO commitments, Priority Sector Lending (PSL) norms, and Wholly Owned Subsidiary (WOS) models; relevant in Mains for understanding financial globalization, capital flows, and foreign direct investment in the banking sector.

Evaluate spatial distribution, institutional frameworks, and policy dimensions.
Apply high-yield mnemonics to solve tricky Prelims and Mains questions.

sections.title: Core Foundations & Conceptual Framework
sections.content:
• **Dual Mode of Operation**: Foreign banks operate in India either through **Branch Mode** (as an extension of the parent foreign entity) or as a **Wholly Owned Subsidiary (WOS)** (incorporated locally in India as a separate legal entity).
• **Regulatory Parity**: Under RBI guidelines, foreign banks are subjected to non-discriminatory treatment vis-a-vis domestic banks in terms of prudential norms, asset classification, and capital adequacy.
• **Priority Sector Lending (PSL) Targets**: Foreign banks with 20 and above branches are mandated to meet a total PSL target of **40% of Adjusted Net Bank Credit (ANBC)**, similar to domestic commercial banks, with specific sub-targets for agriculture and weaker sections.
• **Key Metric / Factor**: Capital to Risk-Weighted Assets Ratio (CRAR) compliance under **Basel III norms**, where foreign banks operating in India must maintain minimum capital requirements plus capital conservation buffers.

items.title: Major Geographical Distribution / Regional Hubs
items.content:
• **Metropolitan Clustering**: Heavily concentrated in Tier-1 financial hubs like Mumbai, New Delhi, Bengaluru, and Chennai, focusing on corporate banking, trade finance, and wealth management.
• **Driving Advantages**: Access to multinational corporations (MNCs), high-net-worth individuals (HNWIs), foreign portfolio investors (FPIs), and robust technological infrastructure.

items.title: Challenges, Reforms & Forward Strategy
items.content:
• **Bottlenecks / Issues**: Limited rural and semi-urban penetration, high cost of branch expansion under branch mode, and intense competition from digitally agile domestic private banks.
• **Policy Interventions**: Encouraging WOS conversion, streamlining digital KYC, and aligning prudential regulations with international financial standards (FATF, Basel III).

items.title: Mnemonic for Foreign Bank Entry Modes
items.content:
• **Memory Acronym / Phrase**: **B-W-R** (Banks Want Rooms)
• **Decoded Meaning**: **B**ranch mode, **W**holly Owned Subsidiary (WOS), **R**epresentative office.
• **Prelims Exam Value**: Instantly recalls the three distinct legal modalities through which foreign banks can establish presence in India.

items.title: Retention Rule of Thumb
items.content: • **Core Formula / Rule**: Foreign banks with less than 20 branches have calibrated PSL targets (historically focused on export credit), while those with 20 or more branches must comply with the standard 40% overall PSL mandate.

upscNotes.content: Examiner Trap: UPSC frequently states that 'Representative Offices of foreign banks are permitted to mobilize retail deposits in India.' This is completely false; representative offices can only undertake liaison and promotional activities, not commercial banking.

Mains Value Addition: In answers dealing with financial sector reforms, argue that incentivizing Wholly Owned Subsidiaries (WOS) over branch expansion enhances financial stability by ring-fencing domestic assets from international banking shocks.

keyTakeaways: Foreign banks operate in India under dual models: Branch mode or Wholly Owned Subsidiary (WOS) mode, governed strictly by the RBI.
Priority Sector Lending (PSL) norms apply to foreign banks, with specific adjustments based on their branch network size in India.
Representative offices act solely as liaison units and are legally barred from accepting deposits or conducting commercial lending.
